title: The Open Question: Is the Angle Condition Enough?
content: The docstring states the question inherited from the parent (PlatonicSolidsOQ02): the parent verifies all 13 Archimedean vertex types have positive angle defect, but with native_decide and a True-stub classification, and asks whether the angle constraint ALONE pins down the 13. This file answers NO. Positive defect is a real necessary condition — it caps the number of faces at a vertex at five (degree_le_five) — but it is not sufficient: the infinite family [3,3,n] passes the test yet is non-uniform and non-Archimedean. The missing ingredient is global geometric realizability, invisible to a single-vertex angle sum. Everything is over ℚ with norm_num/nlinarith/induction, so it is genuinely axiom-free (no native_decide, hence no Lean.ofReduceBool).
mathContext: Necessary $\ne$ sufficient: $\{v : \mathrm{PositiveDefect}\,v\}$ is infinite, so a finite target (the 13) cannot be its solution set. Convex realizability is the global constraint the angle sum cannot see.

title: The Rational Angle Model and the Triangle Minimum
content: Angles are measured in units of π over ℚ: angleFrac n = 1 − 2/n is the interior angle of a regular n-gon (triangle 1/3, square 1/2, → 1 as n→∞). vertexAngleSum sums angleFrac over a vertex's face list, and PositiveDefect faces := vertexAngleSum faces < 2 captures the angular gap. The key monotonicity fact angleFrac_ge_third proves 1/3 ≤ angleFrac n for n ≥ 3: the equilateral triangle has the smallest interior angle of any regular polygon, established by nlinarith on 2/n ≤ 2/3. Working over ℚ keeps every comparison exact and norm_num-decidable.

title: Necessary Direction: Degree ≤ 5
content: The necessary half. list_sum_lb is a generic induction: if f n ≥ c for every entry of a list, then Σ f ≥ length·c. Specializing to angleFrac with c = 1/3 gives vertexAngleSum_ge: a vertex of degree d has angle sum ≥ d·(1/3). Then degree_le_five combines this with PositiveDefect (sum < 2): d/3 < 2 forces d < 6, hence d ≤ 5 (cast to ℕ, closed by omega). The geometric meaning is exact — six equilateral triangles meet with angle sum exactly 6·(1/3) = 2, a flat tiling with zero defect — so five is the genuine ceiling for positive defect.
mathContext: $\mathrm{vertexAngleSum} \ge \tfrac{d}{3}$ and $< 2 \Rightarrow \tfrac d3 < 2 \Rightarrow d \le 5$. Equality $6\cdot\tfrac13 = 2$ is the flat triangular tiling.

title: All 13 Archimedean Types Pass — Without native_decide
content: archimedeanTypes lists the 13 Archimedean vertex configurations (same data as the parent). all_archimedean_positiveDefect proves each has positive defect by destructuring the membership into 13 cases (rcases ... <;>), substituting, unfolding the angle definitions, and closing each with norm_num over ℚ. This deliberately replaces the parent's native_decide — which trusts kernel reduction via Lean.ofReduceBool and so is NOT axiom-free — with an axiom-free rational computation. It is the foundational upgrade that lets the whole file report only propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound.
mathContext: Each of the 13 types, e.g. $[3,6,6]$: $\tfrac13 + \tfrac23 + \tfrac23 = \tfrac53 < 2$. All checked by `norm_num` over ℚ, no `Lean.ofReduceBool`.

title: The Infinite Witness Family [3, 3, k+4]
content: The counterexample engine. family k = [3,3,k+4] fixes two triangles and grows the third face. family_positiveDefect shows angle sum 1/3 + 1/3 + (1 − 2/n) = 5/3 − 2/n < 5/3 < 2 for all n ≥ 3 (nlinarith). family_injective: distinct k give distinct lists (the third entry k+4 is injective, omega). family_not_archimedean: no member is among the 13 — every length-3 Archimedean type has its second face ≥ 6, but the family's second face is 3 (simp). IsUniform is defined (all faces congruent = Platonic), and family_not_uniform shows no member is uniform since 3 ≠ k+4. So the family is an infinite, injective stream of non-Platonic, non-Archimedean positive-defect vertices.
mathContext: $[3,3,n]$ has angle sum $\tfrac53 - \tfrac2n < \tfrac53 < 2$. Injective in $k$, never uniform ($3 \ne k+4$), never Archimedean (2nd face $3 < 6$).

title: The Answer: Infinitely Many Non-Archimedean Witnesses
content: The payoff theorems use Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem with the injective family. infinitely_many_positiveDefect: the positive-defect set is infinite. infinitely_many_nonArchimedean_positiveDefect (the sharp answer to the open question): even after excluding uniform AND Archimedean types, infinitely many positive-defect vertices remain — so the angle constraint at a single vertex cannot determine the 13; global geometric realizability is the decisive missing ingredient. concrete_witnesses pins the two smallest, [3,3,4] and [3,3,5], each verified positive-defect, non-Archimedean, and non-uniform via the family lemmas at k = 0, 1.
mathContext: $\{v : \mathrm{PositiveDefect}\,v \wedge \neg\mathrm{IsUniform}\,v \wedge v \notin \mathrm{archimedeanTypes}\}$ is infinite. A finite set (the 13) is therefore not characterizable by positive defect alone.
